opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest change is that mathematics has always been bottlenecked by human attention. There are maybe a few tens of thousands of active research mathematicians in the world, and each of us can only seriously think about a handful of problems in a lifetime. So whole regions of mathematics just never get explored, not because they're uninteresting, but because nobody had the time to walk there.

AI can change that in a few ways. First is verification. A huge part of a mathematician's time goes into checking: is this lemma actually true, did I miss an edge case, does this 200-page proof hold together? With formal languages like Lean, a machine can check a proof with complete certainty. If AI systems can generate proofs in a formal language, the cost of trusting a result drops dramatically. You don't need a committee of experts spending two years refereeing a paper.

Second is search. A lot of discovery is trying many things: many conjectures, many constructions, many proof strategies, and most of them fail. Humans are good at intuition but slow at trying things. AI can try millions of approaches, and when it's paired with a verifier, it knows exactly which ones actually work. That combination of generation and verification is what lets you scale.

Third, and this is what excites me most, is the shape of the field itself. Today a mathematician might spend a career deeply understanding one corner. In the future you could imagine a mathematician acting more like an architect or a research director: setting the big questions, deciding what's beautiful and important, and working with AI systems that fill in thousands of intermediate results. Some estimates say the existing body of mathematical knowledge could be formalized and extended far faster than we've ever been able to do by hand.

So I'd put it this way: AI won't replace mathematical taste, the sense of what's worth proving. But it could take us from a world where we explore mathematics one careful step at a time to one where we can map it at a much larger scale. And because math underlies physics, computer science, cryptography, and engineering, I think that change will spill over well beyond mathematics itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes mathematics as constrained by human attention, then predicts AI could explore and extend it at a much larger scale, supporting a shift from scarcity toward abundance.

r002.rationale: It predicts broader exploration and many intermediate results, but does not claim AI could solve every currently unsolved theoretical problem.

r003.rationale: The response predicts larger-scale mathematical exploration, but does not specify exponential growth in discovery.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that we're about to see mathematics go from being a craft practiced by a few thousand people to something closer to an industrial process, and I don't say that with any sadness, because the craft part isn't going away. What changes is the scale.

Right now, if you look at how a research mathematician spends their time, the actual flash of insight, the moment where you see why something is true, is a tiny fraction of the work. Most of it is checking. Grinding through cases. Verifying that lemma 3.2 really does follow from lemma 3.1 under the hypotheses you stated, not the slightly different hypotheses you wrote down in your notebook two weeks ago. A huge amount of mathematical labor is this very careful, very slow bookkeeping, and the cost of that bookkeeping determines how many ideas a person can afford to explore in a lifetime. Most conjectures die not because they're wrong but because nobody had the three months to find out.

What formal verification plus AI does is collapse that cost. If a system can take a half-formed argument and either push it through to a machine-checked proof or tell you exactly where it breaks, then the number of ideas one person can test goes up by orders of magnitude. You stop being rationed by your own patience. And that compounds, because mathematics is cumulative in a way almost no other field is. Every verified result becomes a reliable building block, and the library of what's known and trusted grows much faster than it does today, where things sit in preprints for years with a question mark over them.

I also think it changes who gets to do mathematics. Today a lot of brilliant people are locked out, not because they lack intuition but because they never got the ten years of apprenticeship to learn the formal machinery. If the machinery becomes something you can lean on, then a physicist, an engineer, a curious undergraduate can push on a real open problem and get real feedback. The population of people doing discovery grows, not just the throughput of the existing ones.

Now, the thing I'm careful about is that scale doesn't automatically mean depth. It's easy to imagine a flood of true but uninteresting theorems. Taste, knowing which questions matter and which structures are beautiful, is the part humans still own, and honestly it becomes more valuable, not less, when generation is cheap. So my picture is a kind of division of labor. Humans decide where to dig. The systems do the digging and the shoring up, and they surface the surprising things they hit along the way. And then the human comes back and asks, wait, why is that true, and that question is where the next idea comes from.

So the short version: I think we'll see more mathematics in the next twenty years than in the previous two hundred. Whether it's good mathematics depends on whether we build the tools to serve human curiosity rather than replace it. That's really the whole bet I'm making.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a shift from mathematics as a craft practiced by a few thousand people to a much larger-scale process, with far more mathematics produced.

r002.rationale: It says AI will let people test more ideas and push on open problems, but does not claim that every unsolved theoretical problem could be solved.

r003.rationale: It predicts a large increase and says the effects compound, but does not clearly predict exponential growth in mathematical discovery.

astra-6.text:
I think AI could change both how many mathematical ideas we can explore and who gets to explore them. Right now, a mathematician has to invest a lot of time in testing examples, finding relevant results, and checking whether an approach actually works. If AI can help with those steps reliably, we could pursue many more directions, including ones that initially seem too speculative to justify spending months on.

But the number of theorems we prove isn’t the only measure of discovery. We also care about finding the right definitions, asking good questions, and understanding why seemingly different things are connected. Generating a lot of correct results doesn’t automatically give us that understanding.

What excites me is the possibility of a much faster feedback loop: a person proposes an idea, AI helps explore its consequences, and those consequences suggest a better question. If we can combine that with reliable verification, mathematical discovery could become much larger in scale while still being driven by curiosity and judgment.

r001.rationale: It says AI could let people explore many more mathematical directions and make discovery larger in scale, but does not predict a societal shift from scarcity to abundance.

r002.rationale: It does not claim AI could solve every currently unsolved theoretical mathematics problem.

r003.rationale: It predicts faster feedback and larger scale, but does not describe exponential growth in mathematical discovery.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI could change both how many people participate in mathematical discovery and how much any one person can explore. A mathematician might have an intuition but only have time to work through a few examples. With AI, you could explore many more cases, look for counterexamples, and test whether that intuition is worth pursuing.

The exciting possibility is a feedback loop between generating ideas and checking them rigorously. An AI system could suggest a conjecture or a proof strategy, and formal verification could help establish whether the argument actually works. Of course, checking a proof doesn’t tell you whether the theorem is interesting. Choosing the right questions is still a central part of mathematics.

So I’d hope the change isn’t simply that we produce more theorems. It’s that more people can reach the point where they’re asking original questions, and mathematicians can tackle problems that currently require too much exploration for one person or even one team.

r001.rationale: It describes more participation and exploration, but does not predict a societal shift from scarce to abundant mathematics.

r002.rationale: It says AI could help tackle problems requiring too much exploration, but does not suggest every unsolved theoretical problem could be solved.

r003.rationale: It anticipates more mathematical exploration and discovery, but does not predict exponential growth.
